Porter County layout

Lake Michigan borders Porter County on the north and the Kankakee River on the south, in Indiana's northwest corner. Valparaiso is the seat, Portage is the second city and the biggest by both people and land, and the 2020 census found 173,215 residents. Nine towns fill in the map: Beverly Shores, Burns Harbor, Chesterton, Dune Acres, Hebron, Kouts, Ogden Dunes, Porter and Town of Pines. Twelve townships carry the assessment work: Boone, Center, Jackson, Liberty, Morgan, Pine, Pleasant, Portage, Porter, Union, Washington and Westchester.

A parcel might lie in a city, a town, a township alone or a lakeshore community, and each combination has its own levy mix. A house on the water in Ogden Dunes and a farmhouse near Kouts pay the same county treasurer, yet their statements can look nothing alike.

Which office handles what

Start with the TS-1A that arrives with your bill, then match your problem to one of three county offices.

QuestionOfficeContact
Assessment went upAssessor, 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 211, Valparaiso(219) 465-3460
A deduction dropped offAuditor(219) 465-3445; Auditor@porterco.org
Payment posted wrongTreasurer, 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 209, Valparaiso(219) 465-3470

Rate changes come from the state, so none of these offices can alter the rate. Sellers should also check with the Auditor that the homestead deduction is on file, because a buyer's lender reads the same record.

How and when to pay

Each year has a spring bill due May 10 and a fall bill due November 10, and a weekend or holiday date rolls forward a business day. A bill under $25.00 is billed whole instead of split. Full and partial payments are taken all year, and anything late draws a penalty.

Timeliness is judged by postmark: a correctly addressed envelope stamped by the U.S. Postal Service on or before the due date is on time, and so is one an express carrier received by then. Penalty rules are in Indiana Code 6-1.1-37-10, and your bill shows the calculation on its front.

  • Online through the county's two payment portals: electronic checks carry no extra charge and cards carry a processing fee.
  • By phone or mail, following the county's payment pages. Address mail to the Treasurer, 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 209, Valparaiso, IN 46383, and leave the check unattached to the coupon.
  • At the Treasurer's counter.
  • Through a mortgage, escrow or title company, each of which has its own electronic portfolio system.

An online payment needs at least two days to post, so the lookup page can still show a balance for a bit. Account history updates nightly. Surplus claim forms go out after the June and December settlements if you overpay, and a spring overpayment is applied to the fall amount.

The tax sale and redemption

Unpaid parcels are offered in an online auction on zeusauction.com. An owner who wants a property withdrawn has to get cash or certified funds to the Treasurer at 155 Indiana Avenue, Suite 209 by the cutoff in that year's notice, which falls the day before bidding starts.

A sold property can still be bought back. The price is 110 percent of the minimum bid in the first six months and 115 percent later, with any overbid added along with 5 percent annual interest on it, and with any later taxes the buyer paid. Buyers of certificates in the 2026 sale hold them until Friday, October 22, 2027, and that is the last day to redeem. A sale above the minimum bid with no redemption can leave the former owner of record owed the surplus.

A tax sale payment plan is open to some taxpayers. A property that goes unsold but is pursued for title has a 120 day redemption window. Redemption questions go to the Auditor at (219) 465-3449, and payment plan questions to the Treasurer at taxquestions@porterco.org.

How to appeal your assessment

An appeal opens with Form 130, one per parcel, filed with the assessing official, who is the county Assessor wherever there is no township assessor. For the current assessment, June 15 of the assessment year is the date when the notice went out before May 1. When it went out on or after May 1, the date is June 15 of the year statements are mailed.

A narrower error correction route allows a filing up to three years after the taxes were first due. No evidence is needed to file. Both sides trade what they have at a preliminary informal meeting.

  • When the meeting settles nothing, the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals holds a hearing within 180 days of filing and gives you at least 30 days of notice.
  • From there you can carry the result to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 inside 45 days.
  • The Indiana Tax Court is the last stop, and the same 45 days run from the board's final decision.

Tax caps and the 2025 changes

Indiana caps a bill at a share of gross assessed value. Homesteads that carry the standard deduction stop at 1 percent, other residential and agricultural land at 2 percent, and nonresidential and personal property at 3 percent. Any calculated tax above the cap is wiped out by a circuit breaker credit.

SEA 1, the 2025 reform, is changing the deduction mix. After 2026 the $48,000 standard deduction shrinks every year while the supplemental deduction grows, and a homestead credit of 10 percent of the bill, up to $300, starts in 2026. Results depend on home value, so look at your own statement before you promise a buyer a tax figure.

Selling a Porter County house with taxes due

First, ask the Treasurer for the parcel's balance and decide how it gets paid at closing. Title companies want unpaid tax cleared at the closing table, and a property on the certified list owes the redemption amount, not just the base tax.

  • Compare the bill with the online balance to see whether the spring or fall installment is still open.
  • Find out from the Auditor if a deduction on the parcel ends with the sale.
  • For a house on the tax sale list, get the redemption figure and ask about the payment plan.
  • Report any open appeal to the title company.

A sale that falls between due dates can leave one installment open, so ask the title company how it will be divided at closing. Houses near the lakefront or the South Shore Line stations tend to attract different buyers than rural homes in the south, and that changes how quickly a house sells and how much wear buyers will tolerate.

Cash buyers can close despite a tax problem, because the title company pays the balance or redemption amount from your proceeds and you need not find the money beforehand. With no lender appraisal, a house that needs repairs is priced on its condition and is not held up waiting for a loan.

Frequently asked questions

What are the Porter County property tax due dates?

May 10 for spring and November 10 for fall. If either falls on a weekend or holiday it slides to the next business day, and a postmark dated on or before it counts.

Where do I mail a Porter County tax payment?

Mail the coupon and check to the Treasurer at 155 Indiana Ave, Suite 209, Valparaiso, IN 46383, without stapling or clipping them together. A self-addressed stamped envelope brings back a receipt in about six to eight weeks.

Who do I call about a higher assessment in Porter County?

The Assessor, at (219) 465-3460. A dropped deduction goes to the Auditor at (219) 465-3445, and a misposted payment to the Treasurer at (219) 465-3470.

Can I sell a Porter County house that is on the tax sale list?

Yes. The delinquent tax and costs must be paid first or redeemed afterward. Get the payoff from the Treasurer and the redemption figure from the Auditor, then have the title company list the amount at closing.

How long do I have to appeal an assessment in Porter County?

Usually by June 15 for the current assessment, with the year depending on when your notice was mailed. Error corrections can be filed up to three years after the taxes were first due.

Marion County and its layers of government

Central Indiana's Marion County is home to Indianapolis, which serves as county seat and state capital alike. In 1970 a plan called Unigov combined city and county government. Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and the town of Speedway opted out and stayed separate. A few small included towns, among them Clermont, Homecroft and Williams Creek, keep limited local authority, and school and fire districts were never merged into the consolidated government.

The map is a three by three grid of nine townships: Pike, Washington and Lawrence on top, Wayne, Center and Warren in the middle, Decatur, Perry and Franklin below. Your township, school district and municipality together determine the levies on your bill, which is why neighbors a few miles apart can pay quite different amounts.

A typical house in the county went up in 1972, so roofs, furnaces and sewer lines are coming due for replacement. Owners facing that bill often choose to sell the house as it stands.

What sets a Marion County property tax bill

There is no one flat rate. Your parcel belongs to a taxing district, and that district's rate gets applied to assessed value once deductions and credits come off. A "Review Tax Rates" page on indy.gov, run by the Treasurer, shows the rate for any year.

Three county offices each own a piece of the bill:

  • The Assessor decides assessed values and hears appeals.
  • The Auditor processes the homestead, mortgage and other deductions; the Recorder's deed page sends owners here.
  • The Treasurer mails the bill, collects payment and passes the money to the taxing bodies.

Homestead rules changed under a 2025 state law. For the 2026 assessment date the standard deduction falls to $40,000 from $48,000, then loses another $10,000 each year until it disappears with the 2030 assessment date. Meanwhile the supplemental deduction percentage climbs, reaching 46 percent for taxes payable in 2027, and a new supplemental homestead credit worth 10 percent of the bill, capped at $300, begins in 2026.

Sellers feel this less than buyers do. Whoever buys your house must apply for their own homestead deduction after closing, so their first bill may not look like yours.

Offices, due dates and ways to pay

Two installments a year, spring and fall, with the fall one due November 10. The Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building takes the payments.

OfficeAddress and contactHours and notes
Treasurer200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis, IN 46204; (317) 327-44448 AM to 4:30 PM, Monday to Friday

You have five ways to pay: online, phone, mail, a bank, or at the counter. Logging in to an account lets you set up recurring payments and switch to paperless statements. Around a due date, look at the Treasurer's page first for holiday closings and extended hours.

Late penalties and the tax sale

A payment made within 30 days of the deadline, on a parcel with no earlier balance, carries a 5 percent penalty. Let that window close with tax and penalty unpaid and the rate rises to 10 percent.

Long-delinquent parcels can end up at a tax sale. The county attaches a lien to a home with unpaid taxes and auctions the lien online in the fall. An owner who wants the parcel pulled must clear everything owed before that year's cutoff: taxes, penalties, special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, plus a $325 administration fee. Acceptable payment is cash, a certified check, a cashier's check or a money order. Personal and business checks are refused.

A payment plan, partial payments and paying after a sale each have their own page on the Treasurer's site. Call (317) 327-4444 and ask which one fits your parcel.

How to appeal your assessment

Your appeal is a written Form 130 sent to the Assessor. The June 15 deadline lands in the year the bill is mailed if the notice of assessment went out after May 1, and in the assessment year if it went out earlier.

An informal meeting with the Assessor comes next. When it settles nothing, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals has 180 days from the petition to hold a hearing. After that the road leads to the Indiana Board of Tax Review via Form 131.

While the appeal is open you may pay on last year's assessment with no penalty, under Indiana Code 6-1.1-15-10. Attach a short written explanation for the Treasurer. If you lose, the difference is still due.

Owners hurt by recent flooding can ask for a review by submitting Form 137R, and the Assessor also lists a disaster reassessment petition among its services.

Taxes when you sell a Marion County house

You owe the tax for the stretch you owned the house, and the title company normally settles it at closing. Because Indiana bills in arrears, an installment may still be open the day you close.

Before listing or accepting an offer, collect:

  • Your latest tax statement and parcel number.
  • Proof that the last installment was paid, or the amount still owed.
  • Any pending Form 130 appeal, since it changes what the bill should be.
  • Confirmation from the Treasurer that the parcel is not on the tax sale list.

Transfer paperwork starts at the Assessor. Room W121 stamps deeds and sales disclosures, charging $10 per parcel and $20 per disclosure form, and the stamped deed moves on to the Recorder at $35 per document. The disclosure form itself is built in the Properly online system.

Timing works like this. Ask the Treasurer for the current balance, send it to the title company, and let the title company build the payoff into the closing statement. After closing, the deed goes through the Assessor stamp and the Recorder, and the buyer files for any deductions through the Auditor. Keep copies of every receipt until the closing is done, since they settle a dispute faster than a phone call does.

If the house needs work, a cash sale means you hand over the keys without hiring a contractor, scheduling inspections or answering repair requests. You pick the closing date with the title company, and the offer accounts for the condition. Compare that with the cost of repairs and months of carrying taxes on a house that is not selling.

Back taxes, a lien or an unfinished estate make a house hard to sell on the open market. Selling as-is lets the unpaid balance come out of the price rather than out of your pocket beforehand, and a cash buyer has no lender appraisal or repair list to wait on.

Frequently asked questions

When is Marion County property tax due?

Two installments, spring and fall. The fall one is due November 10, and the Treasurer's page has the spring date and any holiday closings.

Where do I pay Marion County property tax in person?

Visit the Treasurer in the City-County Building, Suite 1001. Regular hours run weekdays from 8 AM to 4:30 PM, and (317) 327-4444 reaches the office.

How late can I file a Marion County assessment appeal?

June 15, either in the assessment year or in the year the bill is mailed, depending on when your notice went out. The Assessor at (317) 327-4907 can tell you which.

Can I stop a Marion County tax sale?

Yes, if you act before the sale by paying everything owed plus the $325 administration fee ahead of the Treasurer's cutoff. After a sale, call the Treasurer to learn your options.

Who stamps a deed in Marion County before it is recorded?

The Assessor, at Room W121. Only then does the deed go to the Recorder. The Assessor's fees are $10 per parcel and $20 for a sales disclosure when required.

Hamilton County overview

Hamilton County lies directly north of Indianapolis, with Noblesville as the county seat. Carmel is the largest city, followed by Fishers and Noblesville, and Arcadia, Atlanta, Cicero, Sheridan and Westfield are towns. The county has nine townships, and Clay Township matches the boundaries of Carmel.

Growth has been steady. Population was 182,740 in 2000, 274,569 in 2010 and 347,467 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 387,036. The northern part is still largely farmland, while suburban development has spread north from Indianapolis. Geist and Morse reservoirs add waterfront homes to the mix, and older areas near downtown Noblesville and Carmel sit beside new construction, so condition varies from block to block.

Which offices handle property tax

Payments go to the treasurer. Deductions and the tax sale belong to the auditor, and values belong to the assessor. The treasurer and auditor work from the Historic Courthouse in downtown Noblesville.

OfficeLocation and contact
Treasurer33 N 9th Street, Suite 112, Noblesville; 317-776-9620; Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
Auditor deductions desk33 N 9th Street, first floor, southwest corner; 317-770-4412
Auditor tax sale desk33 N 9th Street, Suite 214; tax.sale@hamiltoncounty.in.gov

Payment options are online, mail, a visit to the office, or a participating bank. Only the online option takes credit cards. A mailed payment must be postmarked by the due date, and a postage meter stamp is not a postmark. The Historic Courthouse has a drop box at its west doors, and anything left after midnight on the deadline counts as late. Banks that take payments include BMO Bank, Community First Bank of Indiana, Farmers Bank, First Farmers Bank, Horizon Bank, Merchants Bank of Indiana and Star Financial Bank. Bring the tax statement.

The county also offers e-billing and an online portal where owners can see statements, payments, assessed values and property record cards.

How Hamilton County assesses so many homes

Hamilton County had 148,707 parcels at the end of 2024, and the assessor's office does most of the valuation work in house. During 2024, 3,721 new parcels were created from 134 new plats and 75 splits, and 2,588 of them carried new construction. Plats and combinations removed 150 parcels. A land order took effect January 1, 2025.

For 2025, the state's new cost tables, adjusted by a Verified Economic Modifier, significantly affected improvement values. Smaller neighborhoods with little sales data had lagged the market, so some saw large increases, while larger neighborhoods saw little change. The county expected 2025 residential assessments to rise. MIBOR statistics show a 7.2% increase in median single-family sale price from January 2024 to January 2025.

The 2024 cyclical phase reviewed residential property in Washington Township and parts of Noblesville and Fall Creek townships, along with agricultural land in White River, Wayne and Delaware townships. Reviewed commercial neighborhoods included hotels, car dealerships, self-storage and the major downtown redevelopment. When a permit is pulled for an addition or remodel, the property is inspected. Transitional areas where older homes are replaced by new construction may get their own neighborhoods.

How to appeal your assessment

Your appeal is a Form 130 handed to the Hamilton County assessor, with a separate form for every parcel. The date to hit is June 15. Whether that is this year's June or next year's turns on when your Form 11 notice was mailed: before May 1 or after.

Expect an informal meeting with the assessor first. If that does not settle it, the county appeals board owes you a hearing inside 180 days and 30 days of written warning beforehand. Miss the hearing without asking for a continuance and you could be fined $50. Still unhappy afterward? Form 131 sends the dispute to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

Before you file, gather what supports your number: recent sales of similar houses nearby, repair estimates for defects the assessor may not know about, and the property record card from the county portal. Bring them to the informal meeting.

Caps and the homestead deduction

Indiana limits what you owe to a share of gross assessed value: 1% for a homestead, 2% for other residential property and farmland, and 3% for nonresidential and personal property. Only owners with the homestead deduction on file get the 1% limit.

The county's deduction page covers the standard homestead deduction, the over 65 credit, the blind and disabled credit and recorded land contract benefits. Filing by January 15 affects the next bill. After approval, a new filing is generally needed only if you change the deed, marry or change how the property is used. A third-party vendor, Tax Management Associates, may mail letters asking homeowners to clarify eligibility, and the county confirms those letters are legitimate.

The tax sale and your parcel

The auditor runs the county's real property tax sale each year at 33 North 9th Street, in the Second Floor Historic Courtroom, and payments go to the treasurer. The 2026 sale was set for 10 a.m. on a Thursday in October. Call the auditor's tax sale desk for the next date.

  • Want a parcel off the list? Pay the whole amount to the treasurer by noon on the day before the sale. Cash, cashier's check or money order only.
  • The property list is updated each Friday, normally by noon, in the two months before the sale.
  • An owner has three years after a sale to claim surplus funds if the parcel sold for more than the debt.

Penalties build before a sale. Paying late within 30 days, with no earlier delinquency, costs 5%. Anything else costs 10%, and each later installment date piles on a further 10% of the unpaid tax.

Selling with taxes owed

A delinquent parcel can still be sold. The title company takes the unpaid amount out of what you would receive at closing. A short list helps.

  1. Ask the treasurer, at 317-776-9620, for the total owed with penalties.
  2. Check the county's online portal for statements, payments, assessed values and property record cards, and fix anything that looks wrong before you list.
  3. If your parcel is on the sale list, decide whether to pay it off now or close before the sale. Remember the noon cutoff the day before.
  4. Tell the title company about the balance when you open the file.

With a tax sale approaching, a cash buyer who accepts the house in current condition can close quickly. The balance is still paid from the proceeds. Flood damage changes the conversation: buyers will want photos, insurance claims and repair records, and standard homeowners policies generally exclude flood damage, so look at your coverage first.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Hamilton County?

You pay the Hamilton County Treasurer at 33 N 9th Street, Suite 112 in Noblesville, or online. The phone number is 317-776-9620. Credit cards are accepted online only.

Can I sell a flood-damaged house in Hamilton County?

Yes. Many owners sell as-is after a flood. Buyers will ask for photos, insurance claims and repair records, and standard homeowners policies generally exclude flood damage, so check your coverage first.

When is the appeal deadline in Hamilton County?

June 15, filed on Form 130 with the county assessor. The year depends on whether the Form 11 notice came before or after May 1.

What if my Hamilton County parcel is on the tax sale list?

You can remove it by paying the full balance to the treasurer by noon the day before the sale, using certified funds. The list is searchable on the county site and updated on Fridays.

Do I lose my homestead deduction when I sell?

The deduction belongs to the owner who files for it, so the buyer files a new application. The county asks owners to file by January 15 to affect the next bill, and you generally do not reapply unless the deed, marital status or use changes.

St. Joseph County at a glance

Up in north central Indiana against the Michigan border, St. Joseph County has South Bend as its seat and biggest city, with Mishawaka second. Settlers organized it in 1830, and the river that crosses it gives the county its name. Its area is 461 square miles, and it belongs to the Michiana region.

The 2020 census found 272,912 people, and the July 2025 estimate of 272,861 shows almost no change. Owners live in about 69% of homes, valued at a median $192,800 in the 2020 to 2024 survey. The county has 119,768 housing units and 611 building permits were issued in 2025. Owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,291 a month and owners without one pay $479. Median gross rent is $1,062, and median household income is $66,868.

Those are countywide medians. Your bill turns on the assessment for your own parcel. The assessor values each parcel, the treasurer collects, and an Indiana bill stacks county, city and school levies.

Tax calendar and late penalties

EventWhenWhat happens
Spring installmentMay (May 11 in 2026)Paid to the county treasurer
Fall installmentNovember 10Paid to the county treasurer
Payment is late and nothing else is owedPaid within 30 days after the due date5% penalty

A single bill arrives with both installments. Parcels that stay delinquent can be offered at a county tax sale. If you intend to sell, request a payoff figure from the treasurer before settling on a closing date.

How assessment appeals work

The St. Joseph County Assessor, in the County-City Building, sets a value for every parcel. If you think yours is wrong, Indiana's Form 130 starts an appeal. In order:

  • File by June 15. When the notice of assessment went out before May 1, the date is June 15 of the assessment year. If not, it is June 15 of the year the treasurer mails the bill.
  • Use one petition per parcel.
  • The county board that hears these cases, called the PTABOA, has 180 days from filing to hold a hearing and must give at least 30 days' notice.
  • Unhappy with the ruling? Form 131 takes the case to the Indiana Board of Tax Review. That route is also open if 180 days pass without a PTABOA decision.
  • Skipping the hearing without an approved continuance or a timely withdrawal can cost $50.

The existing assessment starts out presumed correct. Where it jumped more than 5% from the previous date, the assessor must prove the number, unless the jump comes from improvements or a change in use.

Assessments in 2025 and 2026

Values lurched in recent years. Nearly 14,000 owners appealed in 2025. For 2026 the assessor reported an average countywide drop of 4%, with about 86% of the county landing on a lower value, and appeals were expected to fall well below the earlier count.

The office changed its method too. Long-time owners in areas such as Notre Dame and New Carlisle now form their own submarkets, so they are not measured against new construction. Land is valued by square footage instead of lot type, and a 20/80 rule puts 20% of value on land and 80% on improvements.

A five-acre lot that an owner bought for $9,000 in 2012 had its land value jump from $14,900 to $57,700. After an appeal the assessor brought it down to nearly $11,000. Appeals work best when the number on the notice conflicts with the facts about the property.

Selling with taxes owed or an open appeal

At closing the title company works out what you owe and takes it out of your proceeds. How the current-year bill is split with the buyer comes from the purchase agreement, so ask the title company to show you the math before you sign.

  • Call the treasurer's office and ask whether any installment is unpaid.
  • Read the assessed value on your notice and decide if an appeal is still possible.
  • Expect the title search to find liens and open permits, and ask about them yourself first.
  • Put your Form 11 notice and tax bills in the closing folder.

We buy houses in St. Joseph County as-is, even with back taxes, tenants or needed repairs. The title company takes care of title and recording, and you decide whether to take the offer.

Reading your notice each year

Because values moved so much between 2025 and 2026, a notice you set aside last year may now be off in the opposite direction. Anyone planning to sell soon gains from a lower assessment, since it lowers a buyer's carrying costs, and a higher one can be worth contesting before the house is listed. The assessor's office has held public sessions at local libraries before new notices, and those meetings are a place to ask how the submarkets were drawn.

Open the notice the day it arrives. The appeal period runs to a fixed date, and an owner who lets June 15 slide loses the simplest way to fix an error.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy St. Joseph County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which office handles which problem?

  • Value too high or a wrong description of the house: the county assessor, through Form 130.
  • Balance, installments and penalties: the county treasurer.
  • A hearing on your appeal: the PTABOA, which meets after you file.
  • A result you dispute: the Indiana Board of Tax Review, with Form 131.

Sending a question to the wrong office costs days, and the June 15 date does not move. When in doubt, begin with the assessor for anything about value and the treasurer for anything about money owed. Both can tell you which form or payoff letter you need and where to deliver it, and you can ask either one to confirm in writing what you were told by phone.

What to gather before you sell

A little preparation shortens the process, and most of it takes one phone call to the county.

  1. Locate your last tax bill and your Form 11 notice.
  2. Ask the treasurer whether both installments for the year are paid, and request a payoff if anything is open.
  3. Check whether an appeal you filed is still pending, since a pending appeal is worth mentioning to the title company.
  4. List any tenants, liens or repairs the buyer should know about.
  5. Choose the closing date that fits your plans, then confirm it with the title company.

Selling does not require every item to be tidy. A cash buyer can work with back taxes, an unfinished repair or an unresolved appeal, because the title company settles balances at the table. The point of the list is to avoid surprises, which cost sellers more than the underlying problems do.

Frequently asked questions

When are property taxes due in St. Joseph County, Indiana?

Half is due in May and half on November 10, and one bill covers both. The 2026 spring date was May 11.

What is the penalty for paying St. Joseph County property tax late?

Pay within 30 days of the due date, with no back taxes owed, and the penalty is 5%. If tax and penalty remain unpaid after 30 days, it becomes 10%.

How do I appeal my St. Joseph County assessment?

Send Indiana Form 130 to the county assessor, one per parcel, by June 15 of the right year. A PTABOA hearing must follow within 180 days.

Who values my property in St. Joseph County?

The county assessor, in the County-City Building. The county treasurer handles collection.

Can I sell a house in St. Joseph County with unpaid property tax?

Yes. At closing the title company pays the balance from your proceeds, so get a payoff figure from the treasurer first.

Allen County in brief

Twenty townships and four public school systems (East Allen, Fort Wayne Community Schools, Northwest Allen and Southwest Allen) divide the territory. Three rivers meet at Fort Wayne, and the floods of 1913 and 1982 are still remembered. A house on low ground should come with a flood-zone answer from your insurer or the city before you list. A house near an employer or a main road usually draws interest quickly, so condition and a clean tax record count more than location alone.

Who handles property tax and where to pay

The treasurer collects. The county assessor and township assessors set values, and the auditor processes deductions. Phone the treasurer's office to confirm which desk to visit.

  • Counter: Rousseau Centre, 1 E Main St, Suite 104, Fort Wayne. Open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Bring the full statement or a reprint.

  • Night drop: a depository on Main Street, in front of the courthouse's north side.

Due dates and penalties

Two payments cover the year: May 10 and November 10. A weekend date moves to the next business day, and the treasurer's notice names it. Payment counts as on time if it arrives or is postmarked by then.

The state's Department of Local Government Finance sets the late charge. Within 30 days after the date, on a parcel with no back taxes, it is 5%. Past 30 days, or with earlier years unpaid, it is 10%.

If you have an appeal pending, Indiana allows you to keep paying on last year's assessment without penalty.

Before a sale, find out which half is still open. A spring payment made on time can still leave a fall bill for the same year, and that bill is divided between you and the buyer by closing date. Keep payment receipts and a reprint of the bill in your closing folder, and give the buyer's lender a copy if proof of payment is asked for. Those few papers answer most questions the title company raises about what was paid and when, and they spare you a trip to the Rousseau Centre in the middle of closing week.

Limits on how much a bill can rise

Indiana's circuit breaker caps how much tax each class of property can be charged.

The 1% rate holds only for an owner who receives the homestead standard deduction. A rental, or a house that stands empty, usually falls in the 2% class. That is why an inherited house can see its cap move from 1% to 2% once nobody lives there as a homestead.

Challenging an assessment

Use Form 130, one per parcel, and hand it to the assessing official. The date to remember is June 15. It applies to the assessment year when the notice went out before May 1, and to the year the tax bill is mailed when the notice goes out on or after May 1.

  • An informal meeting comes first, where each side shows evidence.
  • Then the county board (PTABOA) holds a hearing, within 180 days of your filing, after at least 30 days of mailed notice.
  • Still unhappy, or no ruling in 180 days? Form 131 goes to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.
  • Beyond that come Tax Court and the Indiana Supreme Court.

The county's number starts out presumed right. Evidence that shifts it includes a recent sale of your house, comparable sales, a purchase offer or an appraisal. When the value jumped more than 5% from the prior date, the assessor carries the burden of proof, unless renovation or a change of use or zoning explains the jump. Skipping a hearing can cost a $50 penalty.

Selling with tax due

Work out which payment is open and who covers it, then ask the title company how the open installment will be divided at closing. Because Indiana bills in arrears, a payment can come due close to your closing date.

  • Request a payoff figure dated the day of closing.
  • Check whether a lender's escrow account made the last payment.
  • Ask the assessor to look at any value increase over 5%.
  • Remember the homestead deduction if you leave before the sale.

An unpaid balance does not stop a sale. It is paid out of your proceeds. Cash buyers skip the lender's appraisal, which helps when a tax balance and repairs are both in play, but the payoff still has to be exact. Ask the treasurer's office for the balance the week you set a date, and check it again just before signing so a late charge that posted in between does not surprise you. Writing down the date and the amount of each call helps if a figure changes.

A simple order: pull your latest statement or print one online; learn whether your mortgage servicer pays from escrow; give the title company your target closing date so it can prorate; and if you have moved out, ask the auditor about the deduction, since an empty house can drop into the 2% class and change the bill.

For an inherited house, the bill may still carry a deceased owner's name. Bring the court papers to the title company early so the payoff, the deed and the sales disclosure form all use the right names.

May 10 and November 10 each year. Pay within 30 days after a date with no back taxes and the late charge is 5%. After that, or with earlier years unpaid, it is 10%.

Through the treasurer's site you can use electronic check, a credit card, PayPal, Venmo, Apple Pay or Google Pay, and processing fees apply. An automated pay line also answers at 844-576-2177.

When must I appeal my Allen County assessment?

File Form 130 by June 15 when the notice came before May 1 of the assessment year. If it came later, the date is June 15 of the year the bill is mailed.

How much can an Allen County bill climb?

Indiana's circuit breaker holds a homestead to 1%, other residential property and farmland to 2%, and nonresidential and personal property to 3%. The 1% homestead rate needs the homestead deduction.

Can I sell an Allen County house while owing tax?

Lake County at a glance

Indiana's northwest corner belongs to Lake County, a Lake Michigan shoreline county that is part of metro Chicago. Crown Point holds the courthouse. Hammond has the most residents at 77,879, while Gary covers the most land.

Steel built the older neighborhoods. Inland Steel started in East Chicago in 1903 and Gary Works followed in 1906. The county peaked at 546,253 people in 1970, and steel jobs shrank from more than 60,000 in the 1960s to roughly 18,000 by 2015. Housing now varies sharply block by block. Crown Point keeps growing while Gary struggles with vacancy, yet both are taxed from the same county rolls. People who inherit or hold damaged houses in the older areas are the ones most likely to ask about selling as-is.

Your school district is part of your tax rate, which is why identical assessed values can yield different bills in Hammond, Gary and Crown Point. Crown Point Community School Corporation covers Center Township, and Merrillville Community School Corporation covers Ross Township.

Expect cold, snowy winters, with extra lake-effect snow near the shore: 39.46 inches of precipitation and 29.3 inches of snow in a typical year, and January lows averaging 14.4 degrees. Madison County at a glance

Madison County is in east central Indiana, and its seat is Anderson. Population in 2020 was 130,129 for the county and 54,788 for Anderson. Besides Anderson, the county has the city of Alexandria and part of Elwood, plus smaller communities such as Ovid and Edgewood Village. The land is nearly flat, with some hills along the White River and Fall Creek.

The median home here is worth $147,700 and was built in 1965. That is an older housing stock, which is worth knowing whether you are arguing about an assessment or trying to sell a house that needs a new roof, furnace or plumbing.

Who handles Madison County property tax

Property tax runs through three offices in Anderson, and each one answers a different question. The Auditor and Treasurer both sit in the Government Center at 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. A wrong turn costs a trip downtown, so find your question in the table first.

Office hours and holiday closings sit on the county's contact page. Ask the Treasurer about a value and you will most likely be sent to the Assessor.

Homestead and other deductions

The Auditor handles the homestead deduction, the over 65 deduction, the blind or disabled deduction and the veteran deduction. You can file online, and the online form asks for your parcel number. Add an email address before you submit so the office can reach you.

Gather these before you sit down to file:

  • Your parcel number, found on the tax bill.
  • An Indiana driver's license.
  • Social Security numbers, last five digits only, for you and a spouse.
  • For the over 65 deduction, an income tax return or a Social Security 1099.

A deduction follows the filer, not the house. The next owner has to apply for a deduction of their own after closing, so a bill that was low for you can come in higher for them. Ask the Auditor what happens to a deduction on your parcel when the deed transfers.

Due dates and penalties

The spring bill is due May 10 and the fall bill November 10, both paid to the county Treasurer. If either date lands on a weekend or holiday, you get the next business day. The county's tax system takes online payments, which is the quickest way to get a receipt.

Miss a due date and the Treasurer adds a 5 percent penalty, as long as you catch up inside 30 days and the parcel carries no older balance. Wait past that window, or have back taxes already, and the penalty doubles to 10 percent.

Fall far enough behind and the parcel heads to the tax sale. Three or more delinquent installments make it eligible, and SRI Services hosts the county's sale listings online. Once a parcel is certified for the sale, it cannot be paid online. The Treasurer takes those payments in person by cashier's check, money order or cash.

Buying a parcel back after a tax sale or commissioners' sale is the Auditor's job, not the Treasurer's. Look at the Auditor's tax sale list before you set a closing date to see how close your parcel is to certification.

How to appeal your assessment

If your value looks too high, put your case on paper. Form 130 is filed with the county assessing official and ends up in front of the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. June 15 is the deadline, and the year it counts toward depends on the date the county mailed your notice.

The process runs in steps:

  1. An informal meeting with the assessing official.
  2. A hearing before the board within 180 days of filing, with notice at least 30 days ahead.
  3. An appeal to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 if you disagree, or if the board does not decide within 180 days.

An appraisal is optional. Recent sales of comparable homes are the best evidence you can bring, and with a county median of $147,700, a sale price near that range is a reasonable reference point if you think your value is too high.

Nobody is penalized for paying on last year's assessed value while an appeal is open. Lose the appeal and the difference comes due, so set that money aside.

What to settle with the county before closing

A handful of phone calls keeps a closing on schedule. Call the Treasurer first and learn which installments are paid. Next, ask the Auditor whether your deductions stop at the sale and whether the parcel is on the tax sale list. If an appeal is pending, tell the Assessor you plan to sell, because the result shapes the bill the buyer inherits.

Quote the parcel number on every call, since it keeps all three offices on the same record. An inherited house also needs papers showing who has authority to sign, and the title company will want them before it books a closing.

Come closing, the title company splits the year's tax between buyer and seller and pays any open balance out of your proceeds. Ask for its figures a few days early and compare them with the Treasurer's, so a mismatch gets fixed before you sign.

Selling a Madison County house

Madison County owners who sell as-is usually point to the age of the house and the repairs it needs: roof, plumbing and furnace costs, inherited homes, tenant problems and repair bills that exceed what the house would bring after fixing. If back taxes are part of the picture, a cash sale lets the title company pay the delinquent amount from the proceeds at closing.

Two waterways matter for flood questions: the White River through northern Anderson and Fall Creek in the south of the county. A house close to either should have its flood zone checked on the survey or the lender's determination.

Pull together your latest tax bill, proof of payment and any appeal paperwork before an offer arrives. Cash buyers skip the lender's appraisal and repair demands, which is where older houses often stall. Title and taxes still have to be settled.

A cash sale also skips the showings, the staging and the weeks spent waiting for a buyer's loan to clear. You pick the closing date with the title company, and you can sell with the repairs undone. The offer reflects the work the house needs, so expect a lower number than a fully fixed house would bring, and weigh that against the months of carrying costs you avoid.

To weigh your options, request a written cash offer and put it next to what a listing would leave you after repairs, showings and holding costs.

Frequently asked questions

When is Madison County property tax due?

Spring and fall installments are due May 10 and November 10. A weekend or holiday pushes the date to the next business day, and payment goes to the Treasurer.

Where is the Madison County Treasurer?

In the Government Center at 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. The county's contact page lists hours and closings.

Can I pay Madison County taxes online?

Yes, the Treasurer takes online payments. A parcel certified for tax sale cannot be paid online and needs a cashier's check, money order or cash in person.

Who handles homestead deductions in Madison County?

The Auditor's Office. Bring the parcel number, an Indiana driver's license and, for most filers, partial Social Security numbers for you and a spouse.

What makes a Madison County property eligible for the tax sale?

Three or more delinquent installments. Listings run online through SRI Services, and buying the parcel back goes through the Auditor.

Posey County in brief

Posey County occupies Indiana's southwestern tip, bounded by the Ohio River to the south and the Wabash to the west, where the state meets Kentucky and Illinois. Mount Vernon holds the title of seat and largest city. New Harmony, Poseyville, Griffin, Cynthiana, Wadesville, Blairsville, Saint Wendel and Parkers Settlement are among the other named places. Population in 2020 was 25,222, and the county is part of the Evansville metro area.

Rural and small-town parcels dominate, which means the land and outbuilding records at the assessor weigh as heavily as the house. The Ports of Indiana-Mount Vernon, a large river port, is the major employer in the county and shapes demand for housing near the river.

Offices and contacts

Which office you call depends on whether you need to pay, claim a deduction or question a value.

TreasurerBills and payments126 E. Third St, Room 211, Mt. Vernon, IN 47620; (812) 838-1316

The Treasurer sits inside the Memorial Coliseum and keeps weekday hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. A county GIS map lets you pull up any parcel on your own.

When and how to pay

Statements are mailed in early April. Collection happens in two parts, one in May and one on November 10, and the county lets you settle both at once in the spring.

Pay late and the state penalty applies: 5 percent in the first 30 days, 10 percent after that. The Treasurer's Office at 126 East Third Street, Room 211, offers several routes:

  • Walk in on a weekday from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Pay online at poseycountytax.com. Cards carry a processor convenience fee and e-checks carry a $1.50 fee.
  • Use the drop box in front of the Coliseum Building.
  • Pay at a United Fidelity Bank or First Bank branch on the county's list.
  • Mail the entire bill, adding a stamped return envelope if you want a receipt.

A bill that shows up even though your mortgage company pays the taxes is a question for the lender. Deductions for the elderly and disabled go through the County Auditor, not the Treasurer.

How assessments work

Values come from the county Assessor, using a January 1 assessment date for real property. Notices arrive in April, and business personal property filings and exemption applications are due May 15.

A quarter of the parcels are reassessed every year, with a statutory deadline of December 31. To contest a value, send Indiana's Form 130 to the assessing official, normally by June 15. Expect an informal meeting and then a hearing before the county board within 180 days. Anyone still unhappy files a Form 131 petition with the Indiana Board of Tax Review within 45 days.

Open your parcel on the GIS map before filing and read the land and outbuilding entries. Wrong acreage or a shed that no longer exists is simple to fix and can move the value.

The tax sale

Parcels with unpaid tax are sold at a public auction, which the county has run in the Hovey House Commissioners' Room and can move online. Ahead of the sale the auditor and treasurer ask the court for judgment. Paying that full judgment before the auction removes a property from the list.

Buying a parcel back costs 110 percent of the minimum bid in the first six months and 115 percent beyond that. Excess bids add 5 percent yearly interest, and later taxes paid by the buyer are added too. Certificates from the 2026 auction can be redeemed until August 31, 2027. The former owner may be entitled to any surplus when a property sells above the minimum and nobody redeems.

Was your parcel in the sale? Get the redemption amount from the Auditor or Treasurer before listing, because the buyer's title company will insist on it.

Flood and storm questions

Low ground and open country both carry weather risk in Posey County. The lowest point in Indiana is where the Wabash meets the Ohio here, and the John T. Myers Locks and Dam on the Ohio was built to handle river traffic and hold back floods. A tornado crossed Harmonie State Park, Blairsville and Saint Wendel on April 2, 2024.

Buyers and insurers ask about flood zone status and any roof or storm damage. An owner with unrepaired wind damage often finds an as-is sale easier than fixing the house first.

Inherited, vacant or behind on taxes

An estate house, a vacant house and a house behind on tax often share one problem, which is that no one has reviewed the paperwork lately. Start with the mail. Ask the Treasurer to confirm where bills are being sent, and use the change of mailing address link on the Treasurer's site if they are still addressed to the former owner.

Next, gather proof of who may sign for the property. A title company will not schedule a closing until that is clear. Then ask the Auditor whether a deduction is still attached to the parcel, because an elderly or disabled deduction ends when the person it covered no longer owns the house.

Finally, put the balance in writing. Ask the Treasurer for the amount due, including any penalty, and ask whether the parcel was on the auction list. A buyer who knows the full figure at the start can price the house honestly, and a seller who knows it is not surprised at closing.

Before you sell a Posey County house

Get the exact tax balance first, then decide how it will be paid at closing. If you inherited the house, check whether the bills are still addressed to the former owner, since the Treasurer's site has a change of mailing address link.

  • Look up the parcel on the county's search and pay tool and print the bill.
  • Ask the Auditor whether any deduction ends with a sale.
  • Check the redemption deadline if the parcel was in the 2026 auction.
  • Walk the property for storm or flood damage a buyer will ask about.

A cash sale can close around these items. The title company takes the delinquent amount from the proceeds, and there is no lender appraisal to wait for. You choose the closing date, and the deed is recorded after closing. Pick your closing date with the title company and ask them to walk you through the settlement statement line by line before you sign. Whether you list or sell for cash, share the facts about taxes and condition early, and put anything you promise in writing.

Frequently asked questions

When are Posey County property taxes due?

The spring installment is due in May and the fall installment on November 10. Both can be paid together in the spring.

What is the penalty for paying Posey County taxes late?

The state penalty is 5 percent for the first 30 days after the deadline and 10 percent after that.

Where is the Posey County Treasurer's Office?

At 126 East Third Street, Room 211, Mt. Vernon, IN 47620, in the Memorial Coliseum. The phone is (812) 838-1316 and hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Can I get my property back after the Posey County tax sale?

Yes, by redeeming before the period ends. For certificates sold in the 2026 auction that date is August 31, 2027, and the cost is 110 percent of the minimum bid in the first six months and 115 percent later, plus the listed extras.

Who handles tax deductions in Posey County?

The County Auditor's Office, at (812) 838-1300, handles property tax deductions, including the elderly and disabled ones.

Johnson County at a glance

Just south of Indianapolis lies Johnson County, 321.79 square miles in the Indianapolis-Carmel-Anderson metro area. Franklin holds the courthouse, and Greenwood is the biggest city. The population was 115,209 in 2000, 139,654 in 2010 and 161,765 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 174,262 is a 7.7% rise over 2020. Owners live in 72.9% of occupied homes.

Rapid growth puts older houses next to new ones. If yours is dated or damaged, you can compare a fast as-is sale with the expense of updating it to compete with new construction nearby.

The township and taxing district decide which levies reach your bill, so check your own parcel rather than a neighbor's. Three public school corporations serve Greenwood (Greenwood Community, Clark-Pleasant Community and Center Grove Community), and Franklin Community Schools covers nearly all of Franklin. School levies differ by district, even for two houses a few blocks apart.

Floods and cold snaps

Franklin has been through floods. Canary Creek, Hurricane Creek and Young's Creek overflowed in 2008 and damaged or destroyed over 100 homes. The city later bought many of those properties and turned them into green space for its parks system.

Cold matters too. New Whiteland recorded Indiana's all-time low, minus 36 degrees Fahrenheit, on January 19, 1994. Tired pipes, an old furnace or a leaky roof can add up to a costly fix before you list. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is lets you skip that work.

How the 2025 state law changed bills

Homestead deductions were reworked by Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025. The standard deduction is $48,000 for taxes payable in 2026, then falls to $40,000 for 2027, $30,000 for 2028, $20,000 for 2029 and $10,000 for 2030, and is gone afterward.

Going the opposite direction, the supplemental deduction climbs from 40% in 2026 to 46% in 2027 and 52% in 2028. There is also a supplemental homestead credit worth the lesser of 10% of the liability or $300, and nobody has to apply for it. What used to be an over-65 deduction is now a credit of up to $150, limited to incomes of $60,000 for a single filer and $70,000 for joint filers, with an application due January 15 of the first year taxes are payable.

Deductions follow the owner who lives there, so a bill can change after a sale. Bills are also capped against gross assessed value at 1% for homesteads, 2% for other residential and farmland, and 3% for everything else. The state's Tax Bill 101 page explains the caps.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals begin with Form 130, filed with the local assessing official, and cover only the current year's assessed value. After an informal conference with the assessor, a denied appeal moves to the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals, and from there to the Indiana Board of Tax Review and the Indiana Tax Court.

June 15 is the deadline. It is June 15 of the assessment year if your notice went out before May 1, and June 15 of the bill-mailing year if it came later. The board has 180 days from filing to hold its hearing. You do not need an appraisal, though one helps, along with a recent sale, comparable sales or an offer to buy.

  • Clerical mistakes, a wrong owner, a missing deduction or an incorrect property description are objective errors. They go on page 2 of Form 130 and can reach back three years of assessments.
  • Refunds also call for Form 17-T.
  • Paying last year's assessed amount during an appeal does not trigger a penalty.

Selling with taxes owed

Tax that is owed stays attached to the parcel, and closing usually pays it from the sale proceeds. Until then penalties keep building. The state tacks on another 10% of what is unpaid the day after each installment date in later years, and the end of the road is a tax sale.

Every party to the transfer signs a sales disclosure form before the deed reaches the county auditor. It goes to the assessor for review, then the auditor processes it and returns it to the assessor, who holds it five years. Deeds and sale contracts for value are covered, as are forced transfers through foreclosure, divorce, court order or probate.

A simple order of calls saves time. Phone the Treasurer for the balance on your installments, the Assessor if the value or a deduction looks wrong, and the Recorder once the title company asks where the deed will be filed. Keep your latest tax bill, your parcel number and any payoff letters in one folder, because the title company will ask for each of them. Having them ready keeps the closing date from slipping.

Once you have sold, ask the Auditor to send later bills elsewhere. A change-of-mailing-address form works for up to five parcels and can be mailed to 86 W Court St, Franklin, emailed to the auditor or faxed to (317) 736-7021.

How a cash sale works

Cash buyers price the house in its current state, and the closing agent can generally pay back tax from the proceeds, so you need not clear the balance beforehand. The steps are identical in Greenwood, Franklin or the townships nearby.

  • Tell the buyer the address and condition, plus any back taxes or liens
  • Get a written cash offer, which you may take or turn down
  • Choose a closing date that suits your move or estate timeline
  • Sign at the title company, which files the deed with the Recorder

If a job change or relocation is behind the sale, you probably have a date to meet, and a cash closing can be scheduled around it. Estate sales follow the same path, since probate transfers fall under the sales disclosure rule.

Frequently asked questions

What are the property tax due dates in Johnson County?

Taxes are paid in two installments, May and November. The county auditor or treasurer can confirm the exact dates for the current year.

Who do I call about a Johnson County assessment?

Call the Johnson County Assessor at (317) 346-4701 on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. The state's Form 11 page also lists (317) 346-4705 for the county.

Does Johnson County have a tax sale?

Indiana law allows counties to sell parcels with unpaid taxes, and unpaid taxes can lead to one. Call the treasurer at (317) 346-4330 to ask whether a parcel is at risk.

Can I sell a Johnson County house in an estate?

Yes. Probate transfers are among the conveyances covered by Indiana's sales disclosure rule, and a title company can record the deed once the paperwork is in order. Any tax due is usually paid from the proceeds at closing.

What is a sales disclosure form?

It is a state form that all parties to a conveyance sign before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The assessor reviews it first, and the form feeds the sales data the state uses to adjust values.

Elkhart County at a glance

Elkhart County is in northern Indiana, right on the Michigan line. Its seat is Goshen, its biggest city is Elkhart, and the smaller towns are Middlebury, Nappanee, Bristol and Wakarusa. Population was 207,047 in 2020 and is estimated at 208,774 for 2025.

Two rivers shape where houses sit. The St. Joseph River is the main waterway, and the Elkhart River runs through Goshen and Dunlap before joining it in the city of Elkhart. A house near either river or on Simonton Lake brings drainage and insurance questions that a farm parcel near Nappanee does not.

RV industry and home sales

Elkhart County calls itself the RV Capital of the World, and the recreational vehicle business drives local household budgets. When plants cut hours, a property tax installment is often one of the first bills to slip. That is how many owners here end up selling with taxes due.

The swings can be sharp. Manufacturing, which covers RV makers and their suppliers, held 49.6% of county jobs in April 2006, fell to 38.4% by April 2009, and climbed back to 46% by April 2016. Unemployment peaked at 18.9% in March 2009 and stood at 3.9% in April 2016. Those are decade-old figures, so read them as a pattern and not a current number. The pattern is why buyers and lenders here pay close attention to how long a house has sat and whether the taxes are current.

How property tax is set

Three county offices share the job. Values and appeals sit with the assessor, tax cap credits are applied by the auditor, and the treasurer bills and collects. Your rate is built from every taxing unit over your parcel: county, city or town, school corporation and so on.

Circuit breaker caps hold your bill to a percentage of gross assessed value without touching the local rate. Anything the rate would charge above the cap is credited back by the auditor.

Property classCap on tax as share of gross assessed value
Homestead1%
Other residential, including rentals2%
Agricultural land2%
Nonresidential and personal property3%

You only get the 1% cap if the homestead standard deduction is on the parcel. Homestead status reaches the dwelling, a garage and one acre of land. Plenty of rural lots here are bigger, and the acreage beyond one falls in the 2% class. The state posts each county's budget order every January, and Elkhart County's 2026 order was issued January 15, 2026.

How the county reassesses houses

About a quarter of the parcels are reviewed each year, which means a new set of townships is looked at every cycle. In the 2024 phase, Baugo, Benton and Cleveland townships had residential and agricultural property reviewed, Concord had most districts reviewed in all classes, and York had commercial and exempt parcels reviewed.

The ratio study that checks those values drew on 2024 sales, January through December, and treated improved residential property township by township because every township had enough sales. A land order sent to the county board on December 3, 2024 took effect January 1, 2025.

  • Every sales disclosure form is checked through phone contacts, aerial maps, field visits, MLS records and CoStar.
  • Permits for all trades go into the county's assessment system. Elkhart, Goshen and Nappanee process their own permits, and the county handles the rest.

A permitted remodel or addition will show up in your assessment, so pull your property record card before listing and get any mistakes corrected early.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals start with Form 130, filed with the Elkhart County assessor, and each parcel needs its own. The filing date is June 15, though the calendar year turns on the Form 11 notice. A notice mailed before May 1 puts the date in that same assessment year. A notice mailed May 1 or later pushes it to the year the tax bill goes out. Never got a notice? Then the tax bill itself serves as one.

Once your petition is in, the assessor sets up an informal sit-down to compare records. Failing that, the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals owes you a hearing inside 180 days, and you are entitled to 30 or more days of written warning. Want to move the date? You need good cause and a request filed 10 days or more beforehand. A no-show with no request can cost $50.

Unhappy with the ruling, or hearing nothing after 180 days? Take it to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131. After that come the Indiana Tax Court and the Indiana Supreme Court. During the appeal, paying on last year's assessment keeps you penalty free, but paying less than that leaves the shortfall delinquent. The state's appeals fact sheet walks through each step.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing tax will not block a closing. Title companies simply collect the balance from your sale proceeds before cutting your check.

Delay raises the price. Indiana Code 6-1.1-37-10 sets the late charge at 5% when you pay inside 30 days of the due date and the parcel has a clean history. Any other late payment is hit with 10%. Each later installment date then adds 10% of the unpaid principal. Because that add-on is figured on the tax alone, earlier penalties do not compound it. Whatever you pay is applied to tax first, penalties second.

  • Request a payoff from the treasurer before you list or take an offer.
  • Confirm with the title company that both the spring and fall installments are covered.
  • Complete the sales disclosure form Indiana requires. A 2021 state memo said a sale closing by December 31 can set up the buyer's homestead deduction for the next year, with the disclosure form doubling as the application. Check current dates with the auditor.

Cash buyers who skip a lender can often close fast and buy the house as it stands, so no repair list and fewer showings. The overdue tax and penalties still come out of your proceeds, so know the figure up front.

Flooding and weather history

Northern Indiana weather wears on roofs and basements. Goshen sees January lows near 17 degrees and July highs near 85, and Elkhart gets around 74 inches of snow a year.

Flooding has a record here. In February 2018 the Elkhart River in Goshen rose to a record 13.2 feet after heavy rain and snowmelt. More than 300 structures were damaged and some residents had to evacuate. If you have repaired water or storm damage, keep the receipts and permits. Buyers and inspectors ask about basement and drainage history on almost every house near the water.

Schools and getting around

Local buyers tend to ask about the school corporation before the street. Elkhart Community Schools covers most of Elkhart city. Concord Community Schools covers the southeast side of Elkhart and northwest Goshen, and Baugo Community Schools covers the southwest side. Goshen Community Schools covers most of Goshen, with small parts covered by Middlebury, Concord and WaNee.

The Indiana Toll Road follows the county's northern edge, with exits at Elkhart, Bristol and Middlebury. U.S. 20 follows the southern edge of Elkhart as the St. Joseph Valley Parkway, and U.S. 6, 33 and 131 also cross the county. The Goshen historic district, on the National Register since 1983, is built around the county courthouse, and older houses there may come with extra buyer questions about upkeep.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I call about property tax in Elkhart County?

Start with the county treasurer for bills and payments and the county assessor for values and appeals. The treasurer's office is in the county building in Goshen. The state information center at 1-800-457-8283 also takes general property tax questions.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Elkhart County?

The deadline is June 15, filed on Form 130 with the county assessor. Which year it falls in depends on whether the Form 11 notice was mailed before or after May 1. File a separate petition for each parcel.

Can I sell my Elkhart County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the unpaid tax and penalties from your proceeds at closing, so the amount comes off what you receive. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer first.

Why did my Elkhart County bill change when my value went up?

Circuit breaker caps limit the bill to 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead, 2% for other residential and farmland, and 3% for nonresidential property. Without the homestead deduction you do not get the 1% cap.

Does a flood or storm repair affect the sale of a house in Elkhart County?

It can. Buyers and inspectors look at past water damage, so keep receipts and permits. The Elkhart River reached a record 13.2 feet in February 2018, and drainage and basement history comes up in most inspections.

Skip bank bill pay checks, since those envelopes rarely get a postmark. If you are selling, pay the bill directly, or hand the title company a copy.

Appealing a Boone County value

Start with Form 130, filed with the Assessor's Office. The county mails assessment notices (Form 11) each spring, and the appeal date, June 15, is printed at the top.

First look at your property record card. A wrong square footage, bathroom count, outbuilding or basement can be fixed through a separate correction of error. Appeals can arrive by email at assessmentappeal@co.boone.in.us, by mail or in person, with evidence attached. If someone other than the owner or a family member files, a signed power of attorney is needed.

  1. After the deadline, the Assessor reviews the appeal and calls you in for a preliminary hearing.
  2. No deal? The Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals (PTABOA) hears it, usually on a Wednesday, and notice comes by mail.
  3. A Form 115 reports the board's decision.
  4. To go further, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review and copy the Assessor.
  5. After that, the Indiana Tax Court is the next level.

Expect any of three outcomes: the value rises, falls or stays put. The PTABOA must hear the case within 180 days of filing, with at least 30 days of notice. The Boone County Assessor appeal page has current forms.

What changes when the house sells

Buyer and seller both sign the state's sales disclosure form, and it goes to the assessor for a look before the auditor ever sees the deed. One form per parcel is the rule, with a single carve-out for contiguous parcels in one taxing district.

Indiana bills a year behind, so a payment can land right around your closing. Expect the title company to split it by closing date, and ask your agent to confirm that in writing.

The homestead deduction moves to the buyer, who must claim it. Past figures were 60% of assessed value up to $48,000. A buyer who closes after the assessment date can qualify by getting a statement or the sales disclosure form to the assessor by December 31 of the purchase year. A January 1, 2025 amendment may have changed the numbers, so check with the Auditor.

If the tax goes unpaid

A payment inside 30 days of the due date carries a 5% penalty when the parcel has no earlier delinquency. Every other late payment carries 10%.

Each further missed installment can add another 10% on the principal. Money applied goes against tax before penalty. Eventually the parcel may be offered at a county tax sale, after which owners generally have a year to redeem. The treasurer can tell you where your parcel stands.

Delinquency does not bar a sale. Tax and penalty are paid from the proceeds, and owners who are several years behind often prefer a straight cash sale to a long listing.

Getting ready to sell

The typical Boone County seller has a tired house, an inheritance, a tenant or a deadline. Whatever the case, run through this list:

  • Compare the value on your Form 11 to what you would take in a sale.
  • Obtain the property record card and correct any mistakes first.
  • Keep the newest tax bill, your mortgage payoff and any estate papers within reach.
  • Get today's balance from the treasurer before choosing a date.

A cash offer for a Boone County house can skip repairs, showings and appraisal delays, with tax proration handled at the title company. Ask for comparable sales close to your own address, since Zionsville and Lebanon can behave like different markets. Then plan the order: confirm the balance, sign the sales disclosure form, and let the title company file the deed with the auditor.

Near a due date, pay online or in person, because a mailed check counts only with a post office postmark. Renters do not alter the bill. For an inherited house, hand the estate papers to the closer early so names on the deed and the payoff agree.

Once you have closed, collect the recorded deed and the final settlement statement and file them with your tax receipts. A later bill that still arrives in your name should be passed to the new owner and reported to the treasurer's office. That small step prevents a penalty notice from reaching you months after the sale.

Frequently asked questions

When is Boone County property tax due?

Half is due May 10 and half November 10. A weekend date moves to the following business day, and a mailed payment needs a postmark by then.

Can I pay by card at the Boone County courthouse?

No. The counter takes cash, checks, cashier checks, certified checks and money orders. Cards work only through the online or phone service, with a fee.

When must a Boone County appeal be filed?

By June 15, as printed on your spring Form 11. Send Form 130 to the Assessor by email, mail or in person.

What does a late Indiana payment cost?

A 5% penalty if paid inside 30 days and the parcel was current before, otherwise 10%. More missed installments can pile on more.

Can I sell with unpaid tax in Boone County?

Yes. The title company pays the balance and penalty from your proceeds. Get the treasurer's exact payoff before the closing date.

Floyd County overview

Floyd County is a small county on the Ohio River, directly across from Louisville, Kentucky, and part of the Louisville metro area. New Albany is both the county seat and the largest city. At about 149 square miles it is the second-smallest county in Indiana by area. Population was 80,484 in 2020 and is estimated at 82,153 for 2025.

The river forms the southern boundary, and part of the county sits in the Knobs, a hilly stretch with dry ridgetops and wet ravines. Older homes near downtown New Albany share the county with new construction, which rose in 2024. Where your lot sits, on a ridge, in a ravine or near the water, will shape how buyers see it.

Flood and storm risk

The Ohio River is the county's biggest weather risk. In January 1937 it reached 60.8 feet at New Albany, and most of the town stood under water for nearly three weeks. New Albany then became the first city in the region to build flood walls. A tornado on March 23, 1917 killed at least 46 people on the north side of the city.

Hillside lots in the Knobs deserve a hard look at drainage before you list. A few steps help any seller here:

  • Ask your insurer whether the parcel is in a mapped flood zone.
  • Keep repair records for any basement or foundation water work.
  • Expect buyers to ask about roof age on older New Albany houses.

Who handles property tax

Three offices share the work, and all three are in New Albany. The treasurer collects, the assessor values, and the auditor handles rates, calculations and deduction forms. Call before you drive over, since the treasurer's in-person payment counter can be reached at either address shown below.

How Floyd County values a house

  • A neighborhood with too few sales was grouped with a neighbor of similar economics.
  • A land order went to the county board on February 4, 2025 and took effect that day.

Form 11, the notice of assessment, is mailed by April 30 each year. If the notice shows an error, such as a garage that was torn down or the wrong square footage, you can correct it on page 1 and section III of page 2 of Form 130, the same form used for appeals.

Tax caps and appeals

Indiana limits tax to 1% of gross assessed value on a homestead and 2% on other residential property and farmland. Nonresidential and personal property are capped at 3%. The 1% cap depends on having the homestead standard deduction, and a homestead means the house, a garage and up to one acre.

To appeal, file Form 130 with the Floyd County assessor by June 15. The assessor meets with you informally, and the appeals board, which has three members, must hold a hearing within 180 days with at least 30 days of written notice. A written continuance request is due 10 days before the hearing. If the board rules against you or sits past 180 days, take the case to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

While a case is pending you may pay on last year's assessment. Paying less than that makes the installment delinquent, and penalties apply.

Checklist before you list

A little groundwork keeps a Floyd County sale on schedule.

  2. Pull your Form 11 and compare the square footage, garage and outbuildings with what you actually have. Errors can be fixed through the assessor's office.
  3. Confirm with the auditor that the homestead standard deduction is on the parcel.
  4. Ask your insurer about flood zone status if the house is anywhere near the river, and gather repair records for any water work.
  5. Tell the title company early if taxes are owed, so the payoff is built into the closing statement from the start.

A county tax sale offers parcels with delinquent taxes to bidders. Floyd County runs its sale entirely online. Bidders register at sriservices.com, and parcel details are on lowtaxinfo.com/floydcounty. Call the treasurer for the next sale date.

An owner who wants a parcel off the list pays the treasurer directly. For parcels eligible for the sale, online and credit card payments are not accepted, so bring cash in exact change or certified funds. The auditor's office keeps tax sale notices, tax sale appeals, records of sale and deeds.

Debt grows before a sale. A late payment draws 5% if made within 30 days with no earlier delinquency, and 10% in other cases. Each later installment date adds another 10% of the unpaid principal, and payments go to tax first, penalties second.

If you sell before the sale date, the title company normally clears the whole balance from your proceeds. Order a payoff from the treasurer early, because the figure changes with each installment date. Who collects property tax in Floyd County?

The Floyd County Treasurer collects it, and the office is in New Albany. Call (812) 948-5477, option 4 for tax payments, to confirm the right address first.

When is the appeal deadline in Floyd County?

June 15, on Form 130 filed with the Floyd County Assessor. Notices of assessment are mailed by April 30.

Can a Floyd County house be sold with back taxes owed?

Yes. The title company pays the back tax and penalties from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the treasurer for the current balance so you know what to expect.

How much is the late penalty in Floyd County?

It is 5% if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no earlier delinquency, and 10% in other cases. State law adds another 10% of the unpaid tax at later installment dates.

Does the Ohio River affect selling a house in Floyd County?

It can. The river forms the county's southern edge and flooded most of New Albany in 1937. A buyer or lender may ask about flood zone status and insurance for homes near the water.

Howard County overview

Kokomo anchors Howard County, a north central Indiana county of 293.92 square miles. It is the seat of government and the biggest city, with Greentown, Russiaville and Indian Heights as the other names you hear. The 2020 census put the population at 83,658, and about 74 percent of residents live in urban areas.

Manufacturing, automotive work in particular, is the backbone of local employment. Stellantis runs a transmission plant, the Indiana Transmission plants and a casting plant here, a Kokomo engine plant started production in 2022, and StarPlus Energy, a joint venture of Stellantis and Samsung SDI, is in town as well. Many households rely on a handful of plants, so plant news moves housing demand.

Storm history and house condition

Tornadoes have left their mark. On April 11, 1965 an F4 storm hit south Kokomo and killed 25 people in the area. Two tornadoes hit the north side on April 20, 2004. On August 24, 2016, an EF3 tornado damaged about 1,000 homes on the south side and destroyed 80.

Yearly averages are 44.4 inches of precipitation and 34.1 inches of snow. Leftover storm damage, an aging roof or a half-finished repair will turn up at the appraisal and the buyer's inspection. Either fix it first or expect to discount for it.

Offices that handle property tax

Look for all three tax offices inside the Howard County Administration Center at 220 North Main Street, Kokomo. Each is open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

  • Assessor, 765-456-2211: assessed values, Form 130 appeals and exemption applications on Form 136.
  • Auditor, 765-456-2215 (tax line 765-456-2216): homestead deduction filings and tax sale listings.
