Caps and the homestead deduction

Your rate does not tell you what you will pay. Indiana also puts a ceiling on each parcel, measured against its gross assessed value.

  • Other residential, such as a single-family house without a homestead claim or a building with two or more dwelling units: 2 percent

Sign and date a homestead application by December 31. One filing carries forward year to year until the property is sold, the title changes or the contract is paid off. A buyer therefore has to apply on their own, since the seller's deduction stays behind.

How to appeal your assessment

An appeal begins with Form 130, one petition for each parcel, delivered to the assessing official. June 15 is the cutoff, but the year follows the notice. A Form 11 mailed ahead of May 1 means June 15 of that assessment year. A later mailing means June 15 of the year your bill is sent.

The assessor first sets a preliminary informal meeting and then reports back to the county board. You should get a board hearing within 180 days of filing, announced by mail at least 30 days early. Dissatisfied, or still waiting after 180 days? File Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

Two points favor the owner. When the value jumped by more than 5 percent from the prior assessment date, the assessor has to prove it, unless renovation, new improvements or a change in use caused the jump. And paying on last year's assessment during the appeal is penalty free until the case ends.

Delinquent parcels are offered at a yearly tax sale held in the Commissioners' Meeting Room, with a possible switch to online bidding. The minimum bid covers back taxes and special assessments, the current sale-year taxes, penalties, $25 for postage and publication, and county costs. Even after a sale the owner can redeem:

Not sure which window to walk up to? Start with the Auditor, whose staff can point you to the Treasurer or the Plat Room. Bring your latest tax statement, a photo ID, and for a mortgage deduction the signed forms and your loan papers. A short visit before you list can turn up a wrong name, a missing deduction or an old address on the parcel record, all of which are far cheaper to fix before an offer is in hand than during the closing week.

When taxes are due

Spring and fall installments fall on May 10 and November 10, or the next business day when a holiday or weekend intervenes. A bill paid within 30 days after the due date, on a parcel with no earlier delinquency, carries a 5% penalty. Every other late bill carries 10%.

Check the name and address on your statement before you list. If the statement goes to an old address, a missed notice becomes a penalty that comes out of your sale proceeds.

Appealing the assessment

Form 130 starts a challenge, and each parcel needs its own. Turn it in by June 15, counting from the year the county mails the assessment notice, or from the year the bill goes out if no notice was sent.

You first meet the assessor informally, and the result goes before the county's Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals, which owes you a hearing inside 180 days and a mailed notice 30 days ahead of it. If you still disagree, take it to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

Evidence that works: a recent appraisal, sales of similar nearby houses, and photos or estimates for repairs. Start at the Assessor's office with the property card, because a wrong square footage or a structure that was torn down is the easiest error to fix.

Homestead deduction

A homestead deduction can shrink a bill as much as a lower valuation does. The standard deduction has been 60% of assessed value, up to $48,000, filed by January 5. The rule was amended effective January 1, 2025, so confirm today's numbers with the Auditor.

The deduction does not travel with the house. The new owner has to claim it, and a rental or an empty home can fall into a higher class, so do not promise a buyer that your current bill will carry over.

Ask the Auditor which deductions are on your parcel today and print the list. A buyer's lender will want to see the real annual cost, and if you tell them your numbers without a printout they may assume the figure drops once the new owner takes over. Telling a buyer early that the deduction must be filed again in their name keeps the deal honest and avoids a dispute over a bill that arrives after the sale.

Tax sales and surplus

If a Delaware County parcel sells at a tax sale and the price exceeds what was owed, the extra money is surplus. Only the owner whose property was sold can collect it. Anyone else, including an agent with a power of attorney, has to petition the court.

Surplus is released only after the court issues a tax deed and the deed is recorded at the Delaware County Recorder's Office. Call the Auditor at 765-747-7717 with questions.

Selling before the sale keeps the house out of a certificate holder's hands and stops added costs.

Selling with taxes or other issues

Older houses, inherited property and rental units make up many Delaware County sales. Before the deed is passed to the auditor, the state's sales disclosure form must be completed, one per parcel.

  • Ask for a written payoff covering tax and any penalties.
  • Make sure the bill goes to an address you actually check.
  • Pull together estate paperwork if the owner has died.
  • Weigh whether repairs will pay back before you list.

Cash buyers skip the lender appraisal, and the title company settles taxes out of your proceeds.

In practice, call the Auditor to confirm the balance, make sure statements are reaching you, and tell the title company early about any reverse mortgage or other lien. A seller with several rental parcels should hand the closing agent the full list on day one, since each needs its own disclosure form.

If the owner has died, bring the estate papers and deed history. The Assessor's property card shows some transfers, which lets a title company see whether names line up before the sale record is filed.

Plan the last week carefully. Request an updated payoff right before signing, because a penalty that posted after your first call changes the figure. Keep the receipts for any installment you paid this year, and give the buyer's side a copy of the latest bill so the proration at the table matches what you actually owe.

Frequently asked questions

When are Delaware County property taxes due?

On or before May 10 and November 10 each year, and the date shifts when it falls on a weekend or holiday.

Where do I change the mailing address on my Delaware County tax bill?

At the Auditor's office, 100 West Main Street, Room 103, Muncie, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The phone is 765-747-7717.

Who can claim surplus from a Delaware County tax sale?

Only the owner whose property was sold. Anyone else must petition the court, even with a power of attorney, and the money is available once a tax deed is issued and recorded.

What is the deadline to appeal a Delaware County assessment?

June 15 of the year the notice or tax bill is mailed, on Form 130, one petition per parcel. Your notice shows the exact date.

Can I sell a Delaware County house with back taxes?

Yes. Unpaid taxes and penalties come out of your proceeds at closing, and a cash sale can close before a tax sale happens.

Owen County in brief

You will find Owen County in southwest central Indiana. Its seat, Spencer, is also its biggest town, and Gosport is the one other incorporated town. A 2020 head count put the county at 21,321 and Spencer at 2,454. Thirteen townships divide the land: Clay, Franklin, Harrison, Jackson, Jefferson, Jennings, Lafayette, Marion, Montgomery, Morgan, Taylor, Washington and Wayne.

Hilly, wooded country along the White River gives the county a mix of in-town lots and rural parcels. Selling here means working in a small market, and every property tax office is under one roof in the courthouse.

Property tax offices

Three offices share the Historic Courthouse at 60 S. Main Street, Spencer, IN 47460. Pick the one that matches your question.

OfficeResponsibilityContact
AssessorAssessed values and Form 130 appealsRoom 100; (812) 829-5018
AuditorHomestead, over 65 and other deductions(812) 829-5000
TreasurerBilling, collection and the yearly tax sale(812) 829-5011; Treasurer@owencounty.in.gov

The Treasurer is open weekdays from 8 a.m. to noon and again from 1 to 4 p.m., and closes for legal holidays. A quick call to confirm the room and the right line beats a wasted drive.

Value is set each January 1, and the Assessor's office estimates market value in use for more than 17,000 parcels. Changes made afterward usually count from the next January 1. Natural disasters are the exception.

Due dates and ways to pay

The county collects in two parts, one in May and one on November 10. If you mail a check, the postmark has to be dated on or before the due date. A date from a postage meter is not a postmark.

Choose any of these routes:

  • Municipay, the county's online portal, where several parcels can go in one payment.
  • Mail, with the check written to "Treasurer of Owen County" and your parcel number on the memo line.
  • The counter in the courthouse, which takes cash, a cashier's check, a money order, a personal check or a card.
  • The drop box by the north doors of the courthouse. A payment is on time if it is inside before midnight on the due date.
  • The phone line, 812-678-7599.
  • The Spencer branch of The Peoples State Bank, which accepts payments in the run-up to the fall deadline. Its doors close earlier than the Treasurer's, so plan ahead.

Paying by card adds 2.25 percent, with a $3.00 floor. An online e-check carries a flat $0.50 charge. Late payments draw the state penalty: 5 percent when paid inside 30 days, 10 percent afterward.

The Owen County tax sale

Parcels with unpaid tax can go to the yearly real estate tax sale. The Treasurer runs it online through sriservices.com in the fall, and chasing delinquent tax is part of that office's job.

Avoiding a sale means paying the account up to date before the sale day. Request an exact payoff figure, because penalties and costs sit on top of the base tax. If the date has already gone by, call 812-829-5011 and ask whether your parcel sold and what you can still do.

Bring the sale date and the parcel number when you call, and write down who you spoke with and what they quoted. Payoff figures change as penalties and costs are added, so ask how long the quote holds and request the amount in writing if you can.

Owners who are behind also have the option of selling. A buyer who can close fast lets the title company take the delinquent amount out of your proceeds, so you leave the closing table with the account settled.

How to appeal your assessment

Disagree with your value? Put it in writing on Form 130 and file it with the Assessor. An informal meeting comes first, and the result goes on Form 134, which both sides sign.

When the meeting leaves things unresolved, the assessment board schedules a hearing. It has 180 days from your filing to hold it and must give notice at least 30 days beforehand. You can ask to postpone for good cause no later than 10 days before the hearing, or ask for a ruling without a hearing no later than 20 days before. Withdrawing means you lose the right to continue to the Indiana Board of Tax Review.

The Assessor's page lists a few warnings:

  • You do not need an appraisal.
  • The board may raise a value if the evidence supports it.
  • A $50 penalty can follow a missed hearing without a granted postponement. It stays off the tax bill.

File by June 15. Which year that date falls in depends on whether it is tied to the bill mailing or to the assessment year. You may pay on last year's assessed value until the appeal is decided.

Homestead deductions and recent changes

The Auditor, at (812) 829-5000, processes homestead and other deductions. After closing, the buyer files for their own. If your bill has been low because of a deduction, the next owner's bill may be higher.

A 2025 state law is shrinking the benefit. For the 2026 assessment date the standard homestead deduction is $40,000, compared with $48,000 before, and it keeps stepping down in later years. Before you quote a tax figure to a buyer, ask the Auditor what the parcel qualifies for now.

Selling an Owen County house

Roughly 21,000 people live across 13 townships, so you will be dealing with offices that know the parcels personally. Pull the tax bill and parcel number first. Next, phone the Treasurer to confirm both installments are paid and the parcel is not drifting toward the fall sale.

A cash sale needs a clean title and settled taxes, same as any other. The difference is what falls away: no waiting on lender financing, no appraisal, no repairs demanded by a lender. A house that would struggle to win a mortgage can still sell. You set the closing date, the title company pays any open tax from your proceeds, and the deed is recorded after closing.

Put together a folder for the buyer:

  • The latest tax bill and proof that it was paid.
  • Appeal paperwork, including Form 134 if you held an informal meeting.
  • Estate papers or other proof of who may sign, if the house came to you through an estate.
  • A frank list of repairs you already know about.

Candor helps. A buyer who finds a surprise late tends to renegotiate or walk away, while one who knows the facts at the start can make an offer you can count on. If an offer arrives, read the closing timeline and confirm who pays the recording charges before you agree.

Frequently asked questions

When are Owen County property taxes due?

Payments are due in May and again on November 10. A mailed check needs a postmark on or before the due date.

Where is the Owen County Treasurer's Office?

In the Historic Courthouse, 60 S. Main Street, Spencer, IN 47460. It is open 8 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday.

Is there a drop box for Owen County tax payments?

Yes, by the north doors of the Historic Courthouse. A payment in the box before midnight on the due date is on time, and one after midnight is late.

How do I appeal my Owen County assessment?

File Form 130 in writing with the Assessor. If you still disagree after the board hearing, which must happen within 180 days of filing, you can go to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

What does it cost to pay Owen County taxes by card?

Card payments cost 2.25 percent with a $3.00 minimum, online or at the counter. An online e-check is $0.50.
